Let

\[
\angle ABC=\beta,\qquad \angle ACB=\gamma.
\]

Since \(\angle BAC=60^\circ\),

\[
\beta+\gamma=120^\circ.
\]

Because \(O\) is the circumcenter, \(OB=OC\). Also, the central angle subtending chord \(BC\) is twice the inscribed angle \(\angle BAC\), so

\[
\angle BOC=2\angle BAC=120^\circ.
\]

Thus \(\triangle BOC\) is isosceles with vertex angle \(120^\circ\), giving

\[
\angle BCO=\angle CBO=\frac{180^\circ-120^\circ}{2}=30^\circ.
\]

Now consider \(\triangle BCD\). Since \(C,O,D\) are collinear and \(D\in AB\),

\[
\angle BCD=\angle BCO=30^\circ,
\]
and
\[
\angle CBD=\angle CBA=\beta.
\]

Therefore

\[
\angle BDC=180^\circ-\beta-30^\circ=150^\circ-\beta.
\]

By the Law of Sines in \(\triangle BCD\),

\[
\frac{BD}{\sin 30^\circ}=\frac{BC}{\sin(150^\circ-\beta)},
\]

so

\[
BD=\frac{BC\sin 30^\circ}{\sin(150^\circ-\beta)}.
\]

Similarly, consider \(\triangle CBE\). Since \(B,O,E\) are collinear and \(E\in AC\),

\[
\angle CBE=\angle CBO=30^\circ,
\]
and
\[
\angle BCE=\angle BCA=\gamma.
\]

Thus

\[
\angle BEC=180^\circ-\gamma-30^\circ=150^\circ-\gamma.
\]

By the Law of Sines in \(\triangle CBE\),

\[
\frac{CE}{\sin 30^\circ}=\frac{BC}{\sin(150^\circ-\gamma)},
\]

so

\[
CE=\frac{BC\sin 30^\circ}{\sin(150^\circ-\gamma)}.
\]

But since \(\beta+\gamma=120^\circ\),

\[
(150^\circ-\beta)+(150^\circ-\gamma)=180^\circ,
\]

so

\[
\sin(150^\circ-\beta)=\sin(150^\circ-\gamma).
\]

Therefore,

\[
BD=CE,
\]

and hence

\[
\frac{BD}{CE}=1.
\]

\[
\boxed{1}
\]
